standard_prerequisites: Same chapter theorem-galois-theory (finite fundamental theorem, delivered structure): finite Galois correspondence used throughout without further mention (author's announcement at source lines 3288-3290)

Same chapter lemma-galois-profinite (the profinite topology on Gal(L/K)), lemma-galois-infinite (canonical surjective continuous restriction map Gal(L/K) -> Gal(E/K)), lemma-galois-goes-up, lemma-normal-closure-inside-normal
Topology, Lemma topology-lemma-bijective-map is not used here; the closed subgroup argument uses only the topology definition and finite Galois theory
core_obligations: L is the union of its finite Galois subextensions (lemma-normal-closure-inside-normal); for each such E the restriction Gal(L/K) -> Gal(E/K) is surjective continuous with open kernel, so no element of L setminus K is fixed by G and L^G = K
For any subextension L/M/K, Gal(L/M) is closed in G and L^{Gal(L/M)} = M

Conversely for closed H subset G: the neighbourhoods U_S(g) = {g' in G | g'(s) = g(s) for s in S} all meet H, by reducing to a finite Galois subextension E containing K(S) where L^H intersect E = E^{c(H)} and c(g) in c(H) by finite Galois theory; hence H = Gal(L/L^H) and the correspondence is bijective
Open subgroups are exactly the stabilizers of finite subsets, corresponding to finite subextensions; normal closed H give Galois subextensions via the normal images c(N) in the finite quotients
proof_roadmap: Reduce to finite Galois subextensions and prove L^G = K
Prove Gal(L/M) closed and L^{Gal(L/M)} = M
Prove H = Gal(L/L^H) for closed H via the U_S(g) neighbourhood argument
Settle the open-subgroup and normal-closed-subgroup refinements
